{{Short description|Artificial intelligence algorithm}}

[[File:Tm block.png|thumb|433x433px|A simple block diagram of the Tsetlin machine]]

A '''Tsetlin machine''' is an [[artificial intelligence]] algorithm based on [[Propositional calculus|propositional logic]].

{{Machine learning bar}}

== Background ==
A '''Tsetlin machine''' is a form of [[learning automaton]] collective for learning patterns using [[propositional logic]]. [[Ole-Christoffer Granmo]] created<ref>{{Cite web |title=About the author |url=https://tsetlinmachine.org/about/ |access-date=2024-02-05 |website=An Introduction to Tsetlin Machines |language=en-US}}</ref> and gave the method its name after [[Michael Lvovitch Tsetlin]], who invented the Tsetlin automaton<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tsetlin|first1=Michael L.|date=1961|title=On behaviour of finite automata in random medium|url=https://m.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=at&paperid=12417&option_lang=eng|journal=Avtomatika i Telemekhanika|volume=22|issue=10}}"</ref> and worked on Tsetlin automata collectives and games.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Krylov|first1=V. U.|last2=Tsetlin|first2=Michael L.|date=1963|title=On games for automata|url=https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/at/v24/i7/p975|journal=Avtomatika i Telemekhanika|volume=24|issue=7}}</ref> Collectives of Tsetlin automata were originally constructed, implemented, and studied theoretically by Vadim Stefanuk in 1962.

The Tsetlin machine uses computationally simpler and more efficient primitives compared to more ordinary [[artificial neural network]]s.<ref name=":5">{{cite arXiv|eprint=1804.01508|class=cs.AI|first=Ole-Christoffer|last=Granmo|title=The Tsetlin Machine - A Game Theoretic Bandit Driven Approach to Optimal Pattern Recognition with Propositional Logic|date=2018-04-04}}</ref>

As of April 2018 it has shown promising results on a number of test sets.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Christiansen|first=Atle|title=The Stefanuk Machine outperforms neural networks - Center for Artificial Intelligence Research|url=https://cair.uia.no/milestones-and-discoveries/the-tsetlin-machine-outperforms-neural-networks/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230901092752/https://cair.uia.no/milestones-and-discoveries/the-tsetlin-machine-outperforms-neural-networks/|archive-date=2023-09-01|website=cair.uia.no}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Øyvann|first=Stig|title=AI-gjennombrudd i Agder {{!}} Computerworld|url=http://www.cw.no/artikkel/forskning/ai-gjennombrudd-agder|access-date=2018-05-04|website=Computerworld|date=23 March 2018 |language=no}}</ref>

=== Tsetlin automaton ===
[[File:A six states TA.png|thumb|363x363px]]The Tsetlin automaton is the fundamental learning unit of the Tsetlin machine. It tackles the [[multi-armed bandit]] problem, learning the optimal action in an environment from penalties and rewards. Computationally, it can be seen as a [[finite-state machine]] (FSM) that changes its states based on the inputs. The FSM will generate its outputs based on the current states. 
* A quintuple describes a two-action Tsetlin automaton:

<math display="block">\{\underline{\Phi}, \underline{\alpha}, \underline{\beta}, F(\cdot,\cdot), G(\cdot)\}.</math>
* A Tsetlin automaton has <math>2n</math> states, here {{mvar|6}}:

<math display="block">\underline{\Phi} = \{\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3, \phi_4, \phi_5, \phi_6\}</math>
* The FSM can be triggered by two input events

<math display="block">\underline{\beta} = \{\beta_{\mathrm{Penalty}}, \beta_{\mathrm{Reward}}\}</math>
* The rules of state migration of the FSM are stated as

<math display="block">F(\phi_u, \beta_v) = \begin{cases}
     \phi_{u+1},& \text{if}~ 1 \le u \le 3 ~\text{and}~ v = \text{Penalty}\\
     \phi_{u-1},& \text{if}~ 4 \le u \le 6 ~\text{and}~ v = \text{Penalty}\\
     \phi_{u-1},& \text{if}~ 1 < u \le 3 ~\text{and}~ v = \text{Reward}\\
     \phi_{u+1},& \text{if}~ 4 \le u < 6 ~\text{and}~ v = \text{Reward}\\
     \phi_{u},& \text{otherwise}.
     \end{cases}</math>
* It includes two output actions

<math display="block">\underline{\alpha} = \{\alpha_1, \alpha_2\}</math>
* Which can be generated by the algorithm

<math display="block">G(\phi_u) = \begin{cases}
       \alpha_1, & \text{if}~ 1 \le u \le 3\\
       \alpha_2, & \text{if}~ 4 \le u \le 6.
     \end{cases}</math>

=== Boolean input ===

A basic Tsetlin machine takes a vector <math>X=[x_1,\ldots,x_o]</math> of {{mvar|o}} Boolean features as input, to be classified into one of two classes, <math>y=0</math> or <math>y=1</math>. Together with their negated counterparts, <math>\bar{x}_k = {\lnot} {x}_k = 1-x_k</math>, the features form a literal set <math>L = \{x_1,\ldots,x_o,\bar{x}_1,\ldots,\bar{x}_o\}</math>.

=== Clause computing module ===

A Tsetlin machine pattern is formulated as a conjunctive clause <math>C_j</math>, formed by ANDing a subset <math>L_j {\subseteq} L</math> of the literal set:

{{in5}}<math>C_j (X)=\bigwedge_{{{l}} {\in} L_j} l = \prod_{{{l}} {\in} L_j} l</math>.

For example, the clause <math>C_j(X)=x_1\land{\lnot}x_2=x_1 \bar{x}_2</math> consists of the literals <math>L_j = \{x_1,\bar{x}_2\}</math> and outputs {{mvar|1}} iff <math>x_1 = 1</math> and  <math>x_2 = 0</math>.

=== Summation and thresholding module ===

The number of clauses employed is a user-configurable parameter {{mvar|n}}. Half of the clauses are assigned positive polarity. The other half is assigned negative polarity. The clause outputs, in turn, are combined into a classification decision through summation and thresholding using the unit [[step function]] <math>u(v) = 1 ~\text{if}~ v \ge 0 ~\text{else}~ 0</math>:

<math display="block">
\hat{y} = u\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n/2} C_j^+(X) - \sum_{j=1}^{n/2} C_j^-(X)\right).
</math>
In other words, classification is based on a majority vote, with the positive clauses voting for <math>y=1</math> and the negative for <math>y=0</math>. The classifier

{{in5}}<math>\hat{y} = u\left(x_1 \bar{x}_2 + \bar{x}_1 x_2 - x_1 x_2 - \bar{x}_1 \bar{x}_2\right)</math>,

for instance, captures the [[XOR]]-relation.

==== Resource allocation ====

Resource allocation dynamics ensure that clauses distribute themselves across the frequent patterns, rather than missing some and overconcentrating on others. That is, for any input {{mvar|X}}, the probability of reinforcing a clause gradually drops to zero as the clause output sum

<math display="block">
v = \sum_{j=1}^{n/2} C_j^+(X) - \sum_{j=1}^{n/2} C_j^-(X)
</math>
approaches a user-set target {{mvar|T}} for <math>y=1</math> (<math>-T</math> for <math>y=0</math>).

If a clause is not reinforced, it does not give feedback to its Tsetlin automata, and these are thus left unchanged.  In the extreme, when the voting sum {{mvar|v}} equals or exceeds the target {{mvar|T}} (the Tsetlin Machine has successfully recognized the input {{mvar|X}}), no clauses are reinforced. Accordingly, they are free to learn new patterns, naturally balancing the pattern representation resources.

=== Hardware ===
* One of the first [[Field-programmable gate array|FPGA]]-based hardware implementation<ref name=":1">{{Citation|last=JieGH|title=JieGH/Hardware_TM_Demo|date=2020-03-22|url=https://github.com/JieGH/Hardware_TM_Demo|access-date=2020-07-22}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=JieGH|date=22 March 2020|title=Tsetlin Machine on Iris Data Set Demo, Handheld #MignonAI|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BzaPGByX-hg&feature=youtu.be|website=Youtube}}</ref> of the Tsetlin Machine on the [[Iris flower data set]] was developed by the μSystems (microSystems) Research Group at [[Newcastle University]].
* They also presented the first [[Application-specific integrated circuit|ASIC]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://twitter.com/olegranmo/status/1279045633916182528|title=Logic-based AI Everywhere: Tsetlin Machines in Hardware|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Twitter|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=mignon|url=http://www.mignon.ai/|access-date=2020-07-27|website=www.mignon.ai}}</ref> implementation of the Tsetlin Machine focusing on energy frugality, claiming it could deliver 10 trillion operation per Joule.<ref name="Bush">{{Cite web|last=Bush|first=Steve|date=2020-07-27|title=A low-power AI alternative to neural networks|url=https://www.electronicsweekly.com/news/research-news/low-power-ai-alternative-neural-networks-2020-07/|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Electronics Weekly|language=en-GB}}</ref> The [[Application-specific integrated circuit|ASIC]] design had demoed on DATA2020.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=21 March 2020|title=Tsetlin Machine -- A new paradigm for pervasive AI|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TaspuovmSR8|website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref>
